full_title: MANUEL H. REYES, COMPLAINANT, VS. ATTY. DIOSDADO C. SEBRIO, JR., RESPONDENT.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > A. Legal Ethics (CPRA) > 9. Discipline and Disbarment of Lawyers (Canon VI) > c. Charges and Sanctions
topics: Improper claim of influence or familiarity (Canon I, Sec. 2; Canon II, Sec. 15)
Duty to account for and return client funds (Canon III, Sec. 49)
Failure to pay a just debt as dishonest conduct (Canon II, Sec. 1)
Penalties on a lawyer already disbarred; aggravating circumstances
Return of money linked to the lawyer-client relationship vs. personal loans
doctrine:
A lawyer who tells a client that he has friends in government offices who "will definitely offer a hand" in the client's transaction violates **Canon I, Section 2 and Canon II, Section 15 of the CPRA** (merit-based practice; improper claim of influence or familiarity). **Whether the boast is true, or whether the connections are actually used, is irrelevant; the mere claim of influence consummates the offense** (reiterating *Rodco Consultancy v. Concepcion*, decided under Rule 15.06 of the CPR).

A lawyer who receives money for a specific purpose must account for it and, if it is not used for that purpose, return it promptly; failure to return it upon demand gives rise to a presumption of misappropriation (**Canon III, Section 49**, the successor of Rule 16.01 of the CPR). Accepting payment without rendering the service violates Canon II, Section 1, Canon III, Section 6, and Canon IV, Sections 2, 3, 4, and 6. Failure to pay a just debt is dishonest and deceitful conduct under Canon II, Section 1. Each of these may amount to **gross misconduct, a serious offense** under Canon VI, Section 33(a), punishable under Section 37(a) by disbarment, suspension exceeding six months, or a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00.

When the respondent has already been disbarred, **the Court keeps its jurisdiction over offenses he committed while still a lawyer.** It can no longer impose a second disbarment, but it may still declare the penalty, to be recorded in his file with the Office of the Bar Confidant for consideration if he later petitions to lift the disbarment or seeks judicial clemency. It may also impose fines, which may be increased under Canon VI, Section 39 when aggravating circumstances are present (here, prior administrative liability and lack of remorse). Under Canon VI, Section 37, **the lawyer must return money "intrinsically linked to the lawyer-client relationship," but the Court will not order payment of a personal loan from the complainant**, because a disciplinary case is not a civil action for collection (reiterating *Sosa v. Mendoza* and *Heenan v. Espejo*). The complainant may file a separate civil or criminal action.
facts:
Complainant Manuel Reyes agreed to finance the clearance of a Quezon City property that his friend Danilo Zialcita had bought under a Deed of Absolute Sale dated November 24, 1997. Zialcita introduced respondent Atty. Diosdado Sebrio, Jr., who was to work out clearances with government agencies to facilitate the transfer and registration of the property in Zialcita's name, with fees on a contingency basis once the property was sold. Reyes alleged that Atty. Sebrio claimed to know personally the LRA Administrator and the Register of Deeds of Quezon City and promised to deliver the title within six months.

As shown by handwritten receipts signed by Atty. Sebrio, Reyes paid him PHP 400,000.00 (January 19, 2007), PHP 100,000.00 (January 29, 2007), PHP 70,000.00 (February 2, 2007), PHP 128,000.00 (March 2007), and PHP 72,000.00 in cash plus a PHP 100,000.00 check (April 9, 2007) for LRA expenses and representation. After six months Reyes stopped giving money. Atty. Sebrio then avoided him, and the LRA and the Registry of Deeds did not know him. On June 7, 2007, Atty. Sebrio also borrowed PHP 200,000.00 under a promissory note, promising to deliver a check by June 13, 2007. He never paid or issued the check, despite a final demand letter he received on November 19, 2007.

In his Answer, Atty. Sebrio admitted receiving the amounts (totaling PHP 870,000.00), but called them part of Reyes's commitment to finance PHP 10 million in exchange for a 40% return. He denied claiming to know the LRA Administrator personally, saying instead that he had told Reyes he had friends in the LRA, the Registry of Deeds, the Quezon City Assessor's Office, and the Land Management Bureau "who will definitely offer a hand [in] this transaction." He admitted the loan but blamed a 20% monthly interest that Reyes allegedly demanded, and he denied receiving the demand letter.

The IBP-CBD (Report dated May 13, 2023) found him liable under Rules 1.01, 15.06, and 16.01 of the CPR and recommended a five-year suspension. Because Atty. Sebrio had already been disbarred, the IBP Board of Governors (Resolution dated June 21, 2023) applied the CPRA and recommended instead a fine of PHP 100,000.00 and the return of PHP 870,000.00 and PHP 200,000.00 with legal interest.
issues: Whether respondent is liable for claiming influence or connections in government offices.
Whether respondent is liable for failing to render the services paid for and to account for the money he received.
Whether respondent's failure to pay his loan from complainant is a ground for discipline.
What penalties may be imposed on respondent, who was already disbarred, and whether he may be ordered to return both the advances and the loan.
ruling:
The Court adopted the IBP's findings, applied the CPRA (A.M. No. 22-09-01-SC), and modified the penalty.

**1. Yes, he violated Canon I, Section 2 and Canon II, Section 15 of the CPRA.** He boasted that he had friends in the LRA, the Registry of Deeds, the Assessor's Office, and the LMB "who will definitely offer a hand [in] this transaction." Under *Rodco Consultancy and Maritime Services Corp. v. Concepcion*, whether such boasts are true or whether the lawyer actually uses the connections "is irrelevant"; the offense is consummated by the mere claim of influence, which "inflicts damage to the image of the judiciary." Under *Lim v. Bautista*, lawyers guilty of influence-peddling are unworthy of the title of attorney and may be disbarred.

**2. Yes, he violated Canon II, Section 1; Canon III, Sections 6 and 49; and Canon IV, Sections 2, 3, 4, and 6.** He admitted receiving the money but showed no steps taken and no proof of any legal service performed. As in *Reddi v. Sebrio, Jr.*, he failed to credibly account for the funds. Citing *Professional Services, Inc. v. Rivera*: a lawyer who receives money for a particular purpose must account for how it was spent and, if it was not used for that purpose, return it immediately; failure to return it upon demand creates a presumption of misappropriation. Failure to account or return violates Rule 16.01 of the CPR, now Canon III, Section 49.

**3. Yes, his non-payment of the loan violates Canon II, Section 1.** Prompt payment of financial obligations is a lawyer's duty. Under *Sosa v. Mendoza*, failure to honor a just debt is dishonest and deceitful conduct, and flimsy excuses only confirm the refusal. His excuse (the alleged 20% monthly interest) was unsubstantiated, and bare denials do not overcome the evidence against a lawyer (*Reddi*).

**4. Penalties.** The influence-peddling, the failure to render services, and the failure to account together amount to **gross misconduct, a serious offense under Canon VI, Section 33(a)**, punishable under Section 37(a). Since the Court has disbarred lawyers both for failing to account for money received for unrendered services and for influence-peddling, disbarment is the penalty for this first count. The failure to pay the PHP 200,000.00 loan is a second count of gross misconduct. Because he was already disbarred, a fine of PHP 101,000.00 was deemed appropriate, increased to PHP 150,000.00 under Canon VI, Section 39 because of two aggravating circumstances: his previous administrative liability (disbarment) and his lack of remorse. **A second disbarment can no longer be imposed, but it is recorded in his personal file with the Office of the Bar Confidant** for consideration in any petition to lift the disbarment or for judicial clemency. **The Court may still impose fines because it does not lose jurisdiction over offenses committed by a disbarred lawyer while still a member of the Bar**, so it fined him PHP 150,000.00 for each count.

On restitution, the Court ordered the return of the **PHP 870,000.00** in unutilized advances with 6% interest, since Canon VI, Section 37 requires the return of money "intrinsically linked to the lawyer-client relationship." It **declined to order payment of the PHP 200,000.00 loan**. Following *Sosa v. Mendoza* and *Heenan v. Espejo*, a disciplinary proceeding is not a civil action for collection: it involves no private interest and only determines the lawyer's fitness to remain a member of the Bar. The ruling is without prejudice to any civil or criminal action the complainant may file.
disposition: Respondent was found GUILTY of two counts of Gross Misconduct for violating Canon I, Section 2; Canon II, Sections 1 and 15; Canon III, Sections 6 and 49; and Canon IV, Sections 2, 3, 4, and 6 of the CPRA. The Court imposed DISBARMENT for the first count (with an order striking his name from the Roll of Attorneys) and a FINE of PHP 150,000.00 for the second count. Because he had been previously disbarred, the disbarment may no longer be imposed but should be considered, and the Court instead imposed fines of PHP 150,000.00 for each count, a total of PHP 300,000.00, payable within 10 days from receipt, with proof of payment due within 10 days after paying. He was ORDERED TO RETURN PHP 870,000.00 to complainant with legal interest of 6% per annum from receipt of the Decision until full payment.

bar_questions.q: Mario hired Atty. Lim to have a lost land title reconstituted. Atty. Lim told Mario that he had "close friends" at the Land Registration Authority and the Registry of Deeds who would "definitely help" speed up the process. Mario paid Atty. Lim PHP 500,000.00 for "LRA expenses and representation." A year later nothing had been filed, and Atty. Lim could not explain where the money went. In the disbarment case, Atty. Lim argues that his statement about his friends was harmless puffery because he never actually talked to any LRA official. (a) Is Atty. Lim liable for his statement about his friends? (b) What other violations did he commit, and what may the Court order regarding the PHP 500,000.00?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. The mere claim of influence or connections violates the CPRA, whether or not he actually used them. (b) He also violated the CPRA rules on propriety, fidelity to the client, competence and diligence, and accounting for client funds. Taken together, these acts are gross misconduct warranting disbarment, and the Court may order him to return the unutilized PHP 500,000.00 with legal interest.
alac.legal_basis: Canon I, Section 2 and Canon II, Section 15 of the CPRA prohibit a lawyer from making claims of power, influence, or relationship with any officer of a court, tribunal, or government agency. Whether the boasts are true or the connections actually used is irrelevant; the mere claim consummates the offense. A lawyer who receives money for a specific purpose must account for it and return any unused amount (Canon III, Section 49). Accepting payment without rendering the service also violates Canon II, Section 1, Canon III, Section 6, and Canon IV, Sections 2, 3, 4, and 6. These acts together constitute gross misconduct, a serious offense under Canon VI, Section 33(a), for which disbarment may be imposed under Section 37(a). Money intrinsically linked to the lawyer-client relationship must be returned (Canon VI, Section 37). (Reyes v. Atty. Sebrio, Jr., A.C. No. 14062, April 2, 2025)
alac.application: (a) Atty. Lim's statement that his friends at the LRA and the Registry of Deeds would "definitely help" is a claim of influence. That he never talked to any official is no defense, because the offense is complete upon the claim; it damages public confidence in the integrity of government processes. (b) He received PHP 500,000.00 for a specific purpose, did nothing, and could not account for it, which violates his duties of fidelity, diligence, and accounting. Combined with the influence-peddling, his acts amount to gross misconduct, and the Court has disbarred lawyers for both kinds of acts. Because the money was given for his legal services and related expenses, it is intrinsically linked to the lawyer-client relationship, so the Court may order its return with legal interest.
alac.conclusion: Atty. Lim is liable for gross misconduct and may be disbarred and ordered to return the PHP 500,000.00 with legal interest.

bar_questions.q: Atty. Cruz borrowed PHP 300,000.00 from his client Nena and signed a promissory note in which he promised to deliver a check in payment within a week. He never paid or issued the check despite demand. His only excuse, which he did not prove, was that Nena had demanded usurious interest. Nena filed a disbarment complaint and asked the Supreme Court to order Atty. Cruz to pay her the PHP 300,000.00 with interest. (a) Is Atty. Cruz administratively liable? (b) May the Court order him to pay the loan in the disciplinary case?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. His willful failure to pay a just debt is dishonest and deceitful conduct that may amount to gross misconduct. (b) No. The Court will not order payment of the loan in a disciplinary proceeding, without prejudice to a separate civil or criminal action.
alac.legal_basis: A lawyer shall not engage in unlawful, dishonest, immoral, or deceitful conduct (Canon II, Section 1, CPRA). Prompt payment of financial obligations is a lawyer's duty, and failure to honor a just debt, especially when coupled with flimsy excuses, is dishonest and deceitful conduct. In Reyes v. Atty. Sebrio, Jr. (A.C. No. 14062, April 2, 2025), reneging on a promise to issue a check for a loan and failing to pay it despite demand was gross misconduct under Canon VI, Section 33(a). Under Canon VI, Section 37, the Court orders the return only of money or property intrinsically linked to the lawyer-client relationship. A disciplinary case is not a civil action for collection: it involves no private interest and determines only the lawyer's fitness to remain a member of the Bar (Sosa v. Mendoza, applied in Reyes).
alac.application: (a) Atty. Cruz signed a promissory note, promised a check, and paid nothing despite demand. His excuse about usurious interest is unsubstantiated, so it only confirms his refusal to pay a valid debt. This is dishonest and deceitful conduct that may be treated as gross misconduct. (b) The PHP 300,000.00 is a personal loan, not money received for legal services or client funds entrusted to him for a purpose. The Court will therefore not order its payment in the disbarment case. Nena must file a separate civil action (or a criminal action, if warranted) to collect.
alac.conclusion: Atty. Cruz may be disciplined for failing to pay his debt, but the Court will not order him to pay the loan in the disbarment case.

bar_questions.q: Atty. Dela Paz was disbarred in 2020 in an unrelated case. In 2024, a former client filed a complaint against him for misappropriating client funds in 2018, while he was still a member of the Bar. The Court finds him guilty of gross misconduct, and notes that his pleadings show no remorse. Atty. Dela Paz argues that the Court can no longer discipline him because he is no longer a lawyer. (a) Is he correct? (b) What penalty may the Court impose?

alac.answer: (a) No. The Court keeps its jurisdiction over offenses a disbarred lawyer committed while still a member of the Bar. (b) The Court cannot disbar him again, but it may declare the penalty of disbarment for recording in his file with the Office of the Bar Confidant. It may also impose a fine, increased because of aggravating circumstances, and order the return of the misappropriated funds.
alac.legal_basis: The Court does not lose its exclusive jurisdiction over other offenses committed by a disbarred lawyer while still a member of the profession. A second disbarment can no longer be imposed, but the penalty is recorded in the lawyer's personal file with the Office of the Bar Confidant for consideration if he petitions to lift the disbarment or seeks judicial clemency, and the Court may impose fines. Gross misconduct is a serious offense (Canon VI, Section 33(a), CPRA) punishable under Section 37(a) by, among others, a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00. Under Sections 38 and 39, a finding of previous administrative liability and lack of remorse are aggravating circumstances, and when aggravating circumstances are present with no mitigating ones, the fine may be up to double the maximum. Money intrinsically linked to the lawyer-client relationship must be returned (Section 37). (Reyes v. Atty. Sebrio, Jr., A.C. No. 14062, April 2, 2025)
alac.application: (a) The misappropriation happened in 2018, while Atty. Dela Paz was still a lawyer, so his later disbarment does not remove the Court's power to discipline him for it. (b) His gross misconduct would ordinarily merit disbarment, but he has already been disbarred, so the Court will only declare that penalty and record it for future petitions for reinstatement or clemency. It may also impose a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00, increased because of two aggravating circumstances: his prior disbarment and his lack of remorse. Because the misappropriated money was client funds, the Court may also order him to return it with legal interest.
alac.conclusion: Atty. Dela Paz may still be held liable: the Court will record a disbarment, impose an increased fine, and order restitution of the client's funds.

notes: Respondent's earlier disbarment was in Reddi v. Sebrio, Jr., 597 Phil. 168 (2009), as cited in the decision. The fallo is internally layered: it first imposes disbarment for the first count and a PHP 150,000.00 fine for the second, then states that the disbarment may no longer be imposed but should be considered, and imposes fines of PHP 150,000.00 for each count (total PHP 300,000.00). For the second count, the body first sets a PHP 101,000.00 fine and then increases it to PHP 150,000.00 because of the aggravating circumstances; it does not explain how the same PHP 150,000.00 figure was reached for the first count beyond stating that a fine of PHP 150,000.00 is proper "for each count of gross misconduct, considering the presence of aggravating circumstances." Interest on the PHP 870,000.00 runs from respondent's receipt of the Decision.
